content: UP is Old English upp, hardly changed. On a
verb it lifts the action, or carries it to
the end: to give is to hand over; to give up
is to hand the whole thing over and stop.
give up     beside surrender
set up      beside establish
bring up    beside mention
stir up     beside provoke
The particle can stand apart: gave the fight
up. This is the living layer of English, the
part that never stopped growing: a plain verb
and a direction, and new ones every year.
Surrender names the act from outside. Give up
is the hand opening.
THE NEXT 25 CARDS: verbs with up.
DOWN is Old English of dune, off the hill,
worn to one word. On a verb it lowers the
thing, makes it less, or brings it to a stop:
a car breaks down; a cost is broken down
into its parts.
calm down   beside appease
cut down    beside abate
turn down   beside refuse
track down  beside trace
Abate is itself the Old French abatre, to
beat a thing down: the twin carries the same
picture in a borrowed coat. The particle can
stand apart: turned the offer down.
THE NEXT 22 CARDS: verbs with down.
OUT is Old English ut. On a verb it brings
the thing into the open, or runs it to the
end of its supply: to find is to come upon;
to find out is to bring the truth into view.
Run out, wear out and burn out are the other
side: nothing left inside.
find out    beside discover
carry out   beside execute
hand out    beside issue
rule out    beside bar
Discover is the Old French for taking the
cover off a thing: the same motion, said in
the other layer. The particle can stand
apart: found the truth out.
THE NEXT 23 CARDS: verbs with out.
OFF is Old English of, the same word as of,
said with the weight on it; the spellings
parted later. On a verb it moves the thing
away, takes it off, or cuts it loose: to put
is to place; to put off is to place the
meeting further away in time.
put off     beside defer
call off    beside cancel
break off   beside sever
ward off    beside avert
Defer is the Old French for carrying a thing
further off: the twin says the same. The
particle can stand apart: put the meeting
off. Fend is defend with its head clipped.
THE NEXT 25 CARDS: verbs with off.
IN is Old English in, unchanged. On a verb it
carries the thing inside, or lets it through:
a report is handed in, a newcomer fits in, a
door is kicked in. Into is in with to behind
it, the same motion with a destination named.
give in     beside surrender
hand in     beside deliver
fit in      beside conform
rein in     beside restrain
Give up and give in share a twin, surrender,
and differ by their particle: up ends the
fight, in lets the other side through. The
particle can stand apart: handed the report in.
THE NEXT 24 CARDS: verbs with in.
ON is Old English on. On a verb it keeps the
action going, or sets the weight of one thing
on another: to hold is to grip; to hold on is
to keep gripping, and to keep waiting. Carry
on, keep on, go on, press on: the layer's
own word for continue, four times over.
hold on     beside endure
carry on    beside continue
take on     beside accept
count on    beside depend
Depend is the Old French for hanging one's
weight on a thing; count on, lean on and bank
on all share it. Egg on is the odd one: its
egg is Norse eggja, to urge, not the bird's.
THE NEXT 23 CARDS: verbs with on.
OVER is Old English ofer, the over- of tier 1
set loose behind the verb. It takes the
action across or past a thing, turns it, or
does it again: to get over an illness is to
reach its far side; to start over is to
begin again.
get over    beside recover
hand over   beside surrender
think over  beside consider
talk over   beside debate
Consider is the Old French for weighing a
thing in the mind, and debate for beating an
argument out between two. The particle can
stand apart: talked the plan over.
THE NEXT 23 CARDS: verbs with over.
BACK is Old English baec, the back of the
body; on baec, aback, was the direction, and
the a wore away. On a verb it returns the
thing, holds it in, or draws it away: to give
is to hand over; to give back is to hand it
home again.
hold back    beside restrain
give back    beside restore
fall back    beside retreat
strike back  beside avenge
Recover, the Old French for getting a thing
again, stands behind four of these at once:
get back, win back, bounce back, snap back.
It can stand apart: gave the keys back.
THE NEXT 23 CARDS: verbs with back.
